claims_false: Register (b) THE VERB MACHINE — FALSE AS STATED. The register and the file describe a '2-active -> 3-passive' progression. The passage's actual textual order for verbs predicated of the disputers is SIX verbs, interleaved: yujadiluna (40:69, ACTIVE) -> yusrafun (40:69, PASSIVE) -> kadhdhabu (40:70, ACTIVE) -> ya'lamun (40:70, ACTIVE) -> yushabun (40:71, PASSIVE) -> yusjarun (40:72, PASSIVE). That is 3 active and 3 passive, not 2 and 3, and the first passive precedes two of the actives.

File line 114: 'Three passives in a row.' FALSE as a textual sequence. yusrafun (40:69) is separated from yushabun (40:71) and yusjarun (40:72) by two active verbs (kadhdhabu, ya'lamun) in ayah 70. The three passives are only 'in a row' in the file's own re-ordered list, which is then presented as the passage's design ('the machine of the passage, because its five verbs are arranged with terrifying care', line 102).

File line 106: 'This is the last verb in the passage that the disputers get to perform' (of kadhdhabu). FALSE, and contradicted by the file itself twelve lines later (line 118): ya'lamun follows kadhdhabu in 40:70, is active, and is predicated of the disputers. The file makes that active verb its emotional climax while having just asserted no such verb exists.

The count 'five' is internally inconsistent three ways. (i) Title + line 72 + line 102 assert 'exactly five moving parts' / 'its five verbs'. (ii) The file's own Element Two enumerates six: yujadiluna(1), kadhdhabu(2), yusrafun(3), yushabun(4), yusjarun(5), then calls ya'lamun 'the fifth verb' (line 118) when it is the sixth. (iii) Part 2 line 153 gives a THIRD, incompatible set of five — 'Turned away. Shackled. Dragged. Used as fuel. Knowing.' — which includes 'Shackled' (al-aghlal fi a'naqihim contains no verb) and drops both yujadiluna and kadhdhabu. The passage as a whole contains eight verbs (tara and arsalna additionally, predicated of the Prophet and of Allah).

File line 128: 'its dictionary headword — the base noun the plural is built on — is غِلّ, ghill.' This upgrades a corpus normalisation artifact into a lexicographic derivation, and the lexicography goes the other way. al-Raghib, root غلل: 'فالغل مختص بما يقيد به فيجعل الأعضاء وسطه، وجمعه أغلال' — aghlal is the plural of al-GHULL (the fetter), and he cites 40:71 under exactly that entry. The Leeds LEM:gil~ field merges the homographs غُلّ (collar) and غِلّ (rancour) under one unvocalised headword string; it does not assert that one is built on the other. The register's word 'lemma' is therefore accurate about the corpus but misleading about the language.

File line 130 conflates 7:43 and 15:47. The quoted Arabic 'wa nazana ma fi sudurihim min ghillin' opens both verses, but the continuation the file supplies — 'so they can finally sit as brothers, face to face' — is 15:47 ('إِخْوَٰنًا عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَـٰبِلِينَ'), not 7:43 ('تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهِمُ ٱلْأَنْهَـٰرُ'), which is what the register cites. The file gives no verse number, so a reader cannot detect the fusion.

summary: The register's headline risk-claim — Ghafir's 5 jadal occurrences being the Quran's densest with the next surah at 3 — was counted exhaustively against the Leeds corpus and is EXACTLY TRUE (Ghafir 5 at 40:4/5/35/56/69; next-highest is 3, tied across Surahs 4, 11 and 22). Claims (a), (e) and every individual morphology label also verify against al-Raghib and Leeds. Two claims fail. Claim (b), the '2-active -> 3-passive verb machine', is false: the passage predicates six verbs of the disputers, three active and three passive, interleaved — the first passive (yusrafun, 40:69) precedes two of the actives, so 'three passives in a row' and 'kadhdhabu is the last verb they get to perform' are both false, the latter contradicted by the file's own next paragraph. The file's 'five' is internally inconsistent three separate ways. Claim (c) is true of the Leeds lemma FIELD but false as lexicography: al-Raghib derives aghlal from al-ghull (fetter), not al-ghill (rancour); the corpus merely merges two homographs under one unvocalised headword. The root-level connection the file's spiritual payload actually rests on is sound, so the theological thesis survives while the advertised grammatical architecture does not.

summary: All four enrichment claims verified exactly, several of them stronger than stated. hadab is a ROOT hapax (one row corpus-wide, 21:96). yansilun as a verb occurs exactly twice (21:96, 36:51) with identical parses, and the file correctly scopes the claim to the verb form while separately and correctly citing the noun nasl at 2:205 and 32:8. hatta idha occurs exactly five times in the Dhul-Qarnayn passage at 18:86, 90, 93 and twice in 18:96, with all five English glosses matching the Arabic word for word. Both al-Raghib citations verify verbatim against the Mufradat cache, including the file's claim that Raghib adduces 21:96 itself as his shahid for the running sense of nasala — he does. Every tafsir attribution traces to the correct commentator and the correct Arabic, and the file actually CORRECTED the report's 18:98/18:97 heading offset rather than inheriting it. The load-bearing thesis — that the barrier's opening is the arrival of a promise Dhul-Qarnayn himself called true, not the failure of his work — is grounded in 18:98 and in al-Tabari's and al-Muyassar's own words, and is sound. Adab on the Ya'juj/Ma'juj identification question is not merely clean but exemplary: Theme 4 explicitly refuses any present-day identification and names the temptation as a failure mode. No false claims found.
